item.title: The right device for every role in the AI and hybrid era
item.description:
AI and hybrid work have written new rules for matching a device to a role. Equipping the workforce by persona was once a straightforward exercise: the org chart supplied the groups, a stereotype supplied the requirements, and the model held because most people worked roughly the same way. That no longer holds. AI keeps redrawing what roles need, and hybrid work has scattered where they need it. Together, those two shifts have changed the inputs persona building runs on.

The inputs changed, and the principle held. Smart device fleets still get provisioned by sorting employees into representative types and equipping each accordingly. The older build — a role, a department, a rough sketch — came from a workplace that has since changed shape. The new build starts with the work itself: where it happens, what it demands, what it costs when it stops. The device follows from that, role by role.

Reading each role by the work it does

The new build reads each role against the factors that decide what its device has to do. Where does the work happen — headquarters, home offices, client sites, a hospital floor? What does it demand of hardware at peak — not on an average Tuesday? How much of the day runs through a camera and a headset? What data does the role touch, how fast is it changing, and what does an hour of downtime cost? An hour is not the same hour for a field engineer and a back-office coordinator.

Run that reading across a workforce and the real groupings surface: roles with nothing in common on paper turn out to make the same demands of their devices, and each pattern anchors a standard configuration with a defensible reason behind it. The fleet gets simpler — fewer configurations, better matched, easier to support.

Those questions aren’t a checklist — they’re a sample. The complete reading runs eight dimensions deep.

The eight dimensions behind a well-built persona

  1. Mobility & Environment. Where does the work physically happen — and how often does it move? That answer sets connectivity, durability, battery, and form factor before anyone opens a spec sheet.
  2. Work Demands. What does the role ask of hardware at peak — and where does its AI actually run, on the device or in the cloud? The moments that decide whether a device fits sit at peak load, and averages hide them.
  3. Collaboration Load. How much of the day lives in calls, meetings, and screen shares? For some roles, the camera, audio, and bandwidth are the job, and the device gets chosen around them.
  4. Digital Dexterity. How self-sufficient is the role with technology, and how much support does it generate? Some people turn extra capability into output, and others turn it into tickets. Neither answer is a judgment; both are provisioning facts.
  5. Data & Access Footprint. What systems and data does the role reach, and from where? Two roles with the same hardware needs can carry very different access risk, and the device has to reflect that.
  6. Cost of Disruption. What does an hour of downtime actually cost this role? Reliability spend should follow that math, concentrated where a stoppage hurts most and kept lighter elsewhere.
  7. Volatility. How fast is the role itself changing — new tools, new workflows, new AI in the mix? Fast-moving roles need headroom, and stable ones can skip paying for it.
  8. Security & Compliance. What does the role’s risk profile require the device to enforce, not merely support? Compliance sets a floor, and raw performance does not substitute for it.

Read a role across all eight, and the right device for it stops being a debate.

Persona work is a lifecycle discipline

Rollout is where a persona starts earning its keep, and the work runs on from there. The match has to hold as roles evolve: watched for drift, corrected when the work outgrows the configuration, and closed out cleanly when devices come back at end of life. That’s lifecycle work, and most provisioning models leave it unplanned. MCPC, a managed IT services provider focused on device lifecycle management, has spent more than twenty years there — managing devices from planning and provisioning through support, refresh, and recovery, so the fit that was right on day one is still right in year three.

The bottom line

Persona-based provisioning didn’t get harder. It got deeper — and the organizations that read the work behind each role will run fleets that cost less, support easier, and fit the people using them. The ones that don’t will go on buying good hardware for the wrong desks.

MCPC’s new guidebook — built with HP, Microsoft, and AMD — puts the argument to work as a method, with a step-by-step process for building personas your fleet can run on. Download the full guidebook for all eight dimensions in depth and the questions to ask of each role here.

item.title: Oracle pushes AI deeper into enterprise workflows with Fusion Companion
item.description:
Oracle is adding a new orchestration layer to its Fusion Cloud Applications suite to help enterprises automate business workflows, coordinate AI agents, and execute tasks across applications with less manual intervention.

The new layer, named Fusion Companion, will allow enterprise users to initiate business tasks through external AI assistants such as ChatGPT, rather than navigating individual enterprise applications to find the right workflows or tools, the company said in a statement.

It interprets users’ objectives and coordinates the transactions, workflows, approvals, and AI agents needed to complete tasks, including taking authorized actions across other enterprise systems, the company added.

Companion aims to reduce friction in enterprise AI adoption

That ability to coordinate and complete tasks without manual intervention will result in improved productivity for business users in an enterprise, said Stephanie Walter, practice leader of AI stack at HyperFrame Research.

“Companion’s automation means that an employee does not have to initiate multiple steps separately to complete a particular task. That could replace a sequence of clicks and handoffs with a request and any necessary approvals. It reduces the need to navigate applications, while keeping their business processes in place,” Walter added.

Fusion Companion’s ability to let employees initiate tasks through external AI assistants while keeping execution within enterprise systems could help CIOs address the tension between employees’ growing use of these tools and the need to preserve established business processes, security policies, and approval controls, said Ashish Chaturvedi, executive research leader at HFS Research.

“Access through ChatGPT carries real weight because it meets employees where they already spend their day. Many knowledge workers now open an AI assistant before they open any enterprise application. If you have ever watched a colleague draft an email in ChatGPT and then switch to an ERP screen to copy figures across, you have seen the friction Oracle is trying to remove,” Chaturvedi said.

Walter, meanwhile, sees a potential reduction in integration complexity for CIOs, as Fusion Companion could provide a common orchestration layer for employees to access enterprise workflows through different AI assistants, reducing the need to build and maintain separate integrations for each interface.

Challenges around implementation

However, the implementation of Fusion Companion is not without caveats.

“One of the caveats concerns data movement. When a user works through ChatGPT, some business context has to travel to that external assistant for the conversation to make sense. CIOs, therefore, should want precise answers on what data leaves the Oracle environment, how it is retained, and how this fits with their contracts with OpenAI,” Chaturvedi said.

Another concern is the reliability of intent interpretation, Chaturvedi added: “A well-phrased request will usually map to the correct process, but ambiguous requests could trigger the wrong transaction, and the consequences grow as agents gain authority to act.”

There are also concerns around dependency and erosion of process knowledge among enterprise users.

“When Companion becomes the layer that decides how work flows, including across non-Oracle systems, Oracle gains considerable influence over the enterprise’s process architecture. While that is convenient for Fusion-centric organizations, it could be a concern for those that want to keep orchestration neutral,” Chaturvedi said.

Over time, he added, delegating more work to AI agents could also erode employees’ understanding of underlying business processes, making exceptions and failures harder to diagnose when automated workflows break down.

Alongside Fusion Companion, Oracle is adding Fusion Agentic Home, a native interface within Fusion Applications that serves as an alternative for enterprise users who prefer not to rely on external AI assistants to delegate tasks and manage AI-driven workflows, while using Companion as the underlying orchestration layer.

Both Fusion Companion and Agentic Home are being made available as part of the Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications Release 26D, the company said.

The article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

item.title: ‘Citizen AI’ can help IT leaders spark business solutions — if done right
item.description:
AI fluency has long mattered to Sambit Dutta. When he joined global chemical manufacturer Hexion this year as SVP of AI transformation, his strategy included bringing “AI to the masses, where the people can not only just consume AI, but also become what we call builders.”

Dutta has made citizen AI a cornerstone of Hexion’s IT strategy because he believes that when the creativity and domain expertise of employees is centralized and funneled through a business analyst or developer, “there are always things lost in translation.” Further, “there’s a queuing process where that request ultimately gets queued, and then based on dollars and other priorities, never gets executed,” he adds.

Dutta also believes that innovation unleashed at the grassroots level is how enterprises achieve true transformation. And it facilitates change management because people become more receptive to absorbing technology at that level, he says.

“We firmly believe that we are at a stage where citizen development has finally taken off” at Hexion, Dutton says.

Citizen AI — a development strategy that has CIOs making AI tools available to employees outside IT to create their own solutions — is taking hold inside enterprises. It democratizes AI by enabling business users to solve problems and create efficiencies in their roles without the overhead of full IT-led development.

“Historically, turning a good idea into a technology solution required specialist skills, funding, and space on a development roadmap,” says Ankur Anand, group CIO at technology recruiter Harvey Nash. “AI lowers that barrier. People can explore an idea, create an agent or prototype, and establish whether it genuinely solves a business problem before the organization commits significant resources.”

But the objective isn’t to create hundreds of unofficial production systems, Anand adds. “It’s to create hundreds of experiments and make it much easier for good ideas to emerge from anywhere in the organization.”

Freedom first, governance to follow

Travel tech company eSky Group is one such company moving toward an AI-first model, “where using it is as natural as using email or a browser,” says Piotr Mynarski, technology director there.

“Employees creating their own agents is not a fringe behavior,” he says. “It is one of the clearest trends we see inside innovative companies today, and the most visible change in how our engineering works.”

At the end of 2025, eSky made AI a company objective, and by spring 2026, the company had agreements with several AI providers whose tools were opened up to everyone, not just to engineering staff.

eSky expects about 60% of its more than 650 employees worldwide outside the contact center to become fluent with AI. Regular use of AI is climbing toward 80%, Mynarski says, who notes that the company’s approach was a bit unusual: Company officials “barely capped budgets, let people use the tools for personal purposes, too, and gave everyone room to experiment rather than mandating a narrow toolset,” he says.

That approach deliberately gave employees freedom first, with governance to follow once leaders saw what they actually built.

“That order was a conscious bet and so far, the right one,” Mynarski says. “Today, we have over 30 agents across the company, almost every engineering team works with at least one, and several teams have more, with some already running in production.”

The agents were developed from a shared codebase built by eSky engineers, and they specialize in different needs: development of new products and features, maintenance, analytics, and monitoring business metrics.

“The rules are catching up rather than leading,” Mynarski notes. “Every agent has its own identity and credentials, guardrails and observability are standard, and responsibility for an agent sits with the team that runs it, not with a central AI department.”

AI reduces the barrier to entry — but still requires guardrails

Before joining Hexion, Dutta worked at Nestlé, where he implemented “a pretty robust program around digital fluency.” Parts of the program worked, but some didn’t, particularly where sophistication was required “in thinking, and a little bit of a technical depth.”

Some citizen development can be performed with drag-and-drop tools, but often written instructions are required, he notes. “A lot of people get really scared when you introduce those kinds of concepts to them.” That creates a barrier when employees want to leverage citizen development in areas such as data science, real-time automation, and Microsoft Power Apps, Dutta points out.

“Those are one type of automation that requires a little bit more sophistication,” he says. But that has changed. “The biggest unlock is now with prompt. You can avoid going into the developer tool altogether. … You can simply go in the prompt and describe what you want,and accordingly, the backend generates the application for it.”

As a result, Power Apps, which was more challenging for users to master and scale, no longer requires business users “to know the nuances about how to create a Power app.” Dutta says, unlocking a new level of productivity to a broader range of users.

At Hexion, employees use a centralized IT-owned platform to create agents. Business users have several tool options, “but those options are restricted to what we believe are enterprise-grade tools, and we have to secure it,” Dutta says.

For example, whereas everyone in the company can use Power App Vibe, only some employees have access to AI building platform Replit for coding.

Replit is “a little bit of a clamped-down application because we want to control what goes into production and how it connects with enterprise databases,” Dutta explains. “Replit can be dangerous because it if it is connected to SAP and other critical systems in a way that the users are doing something unusual with their app, it may bring down the system altogether.”

Users can, however, immediately connect the Replit applications they create to a data lake or other repositories, he adds. “It’s only when a transactional system gets impacted that we impose some condition.”

Unlocking business-user creativity

Hexion’s citizen AI strategy is unleashing creativity across the company, Dutta says. For example, the leader for environmental health and safety built an app she calls Wingman that can be used in the company’s factories to run health and safety processes. “We did some light editing on the core to make it a little bit enterprise standard,” and then it was deployed, Dutta says.

Given the divide between vibe-coded apps and production systems, governance remains an essential ingredient of any citizen AI development strategy. One of the AI governance tools Hexion uses is Microsoft Agent 365, which Dutta says lets IT see which agent is running and the various statuses of agents that employees deploy.

“We can start and stop anything we want across the enterprise,” he says. “It’s one single-pane governance layer.”

At eSky, employees are automating their daily work and building small applications for reporting and for automating specific business cases, Mynarski says. They also lean heavily on specialized agents that can take over parts of a job for them, he says.

In one instance, a performance marketing specialist built an agent that reads campaign data across eSky’s markets and is starting to generate ad content. The operations team runs a platform of 16 scheduled automations and small apps for controlling, reconciliation, and refunds, built by the people who used to do that work by hand, he says.

However, “this often becomes a problem the moment a personal tool needs to become a production system,” Mynarski says. “We have that covered with practices and guardrails that these teams can plug into, so the initiative stays with them and the hardening comes from us.”

At Harvey Nash, a content manager has created an agent that helps the company’s recruitment consultants find approved posts and assets, personalize it to their role, and post them to their social channels.

“This supports us with brand amplification and helping position them as market experts without requiring them to create new content,” Anand says. “We can measure the number of posts created, adding a gamification element to it to encourage usage.”

Coding isn’t the most important capability needed to become an AI citizen, he notes. “It’s understanding a problem well enough to describe it, knowing the context and data behind it, and having the judgment to recognize whether the result is useful.”

Overall, citizen AI is about dramatically increasing the number of experiments an organization can undertake, Anand says. “Give people the freedom and guardrails to turn ideas into proof points,” he says. “When an idea demonstrates real value, that’s when technology steps in to make it enterprise-ready and scale it. You get grassroots innovation without creating a technology Wild West.”

For CIOs considering launching a citizen AI strategy, Mynarski advises keeping costs in mind. “You have to ask, more than ever before, whether a given use brings value to the organization, because it is very easy to spin up AI that works beautifully and adds nothing,” he says.

Still, Mynarski believes the issue CIOs face is not employees doing too much with AI without permission. “The challenge is teams doing too little,” he says. “My advice to other CIOs: Talk about security in the same breath as innovation. If you let that gap grow, the freedom you gave people will be taken away from them later, and that is the expensive scenario.”

item.title: The AI notetaker risk is now an everywhere problem
item.description:
The businesspeople adopting AI notetakers are not being reckless. They are responding to a real business need. Our teams are in meetings all day with companies we support, and the idea that we could read a clean summary of every one of them at the end of the day makes us better partners to our customers. At the AI-first startups we spend time with, a new account manager can walk in on day one, inherit the full recorded history of every customer conversation, and ask the AI what that customer actually cares about. That is not surveillance culture for its own sake. It’s a better way to serve people.

Still, AI notetakers present cyber risks, as we have been warning about for the past year: shadow adoption measured in hundreds of accounts in a matter of weeks, vendors without SOC 2 or real encryption, consent liability, litigation exposure. In April, one of us stood on stage at the [un]prompted conference and argued that the most important attendee in your meetings is no longer a person. AI notetakers decide what matters, assigning the action items and providing the summary that becomes the meeting’s official record.

But our early warnings about AI notetakers shared an assumption we no longer hold: that the notetaker joins the meeting. That assumption quietly died this summer, as the notetaker has left the meeting platform and moved onto the body — and policies haven’t noticed let alone caught up to this change yet.

From the meeting to the wrist

On July 28, Granola, the AI notetaker we see most often in our worlds, launched an Apple Watch app. One tap on the wrist and it records whatever happens around you. No bot joining the call, no banner announcing itself, no laptop open on the table.

The same week, DEF CON banned Meta-style smart glasses from the conference floor over recording concerns. Meta, meanwhile, had already acquired Limitless, the AI pendant company, folding always-on personal recording into the largest consumer hardware pipeline in the world. One public company we’ve worked with now screens attendees for smart glasses before all-hands meetings where unreleased plans are discussed.

We’ve tested this ourselves, putting the watch under a jacket sleeve, tapping once, and recording an entire evening walk. Clean transcript. Nobody could have known.

In the United States, recording someone without their permission depends on which state you are standing in. California says you can’t, but many states say you can. More importantly we still have no norms of disclosure, and the hardware is now designed to be invisible.

The record is not neutral

Since the April talk, we have met a steady stream of people telling us how they game these systems. One person described doing prompt injection against a notetaker in a live meeting, right as we walked offstage. Another explained the simplest trick we have heard: join early, and for the five minutes you are alone with the notetakers, calmly narrate the outcomes you want captured as the most important takeaways. A third said he figured out how to silently crash other companies’ notetakers, so the meeting ends and there is no record. There is academic research behind all this. Call it manipulation or call it strategic communication. The methods work.

Notetaking systems also fail on their own. We have watched a transcript mishear one word, then reinterpret the rest of the conversation to fit the error. Colleagues with accents the models handle poorly carry more of that risk than the rest of us. And these tools are no longer stenographers. They have memories. Granola pulls context from prior meetings and background on the people in the meeting into today’s meeting notes. That is useful, but it also means a summary shared outside your company could leak reasoning from meetings the other party was never in.

Then there is the case that should be on every policy writer’s mind. Last November, a Campbell’s security executive was terminated for what they said during a meeting secretly recorded by an employee during what he thought was a private lunch conversation. The recording surfaced months later through an employment lawyer, and the executive was gone within days. Whatever you think of what was said, notice the mechanism: no notetaker bot, no meeting platform. One person, one device, one conversation the speaker believed was off the record. There is no such thing anymore.

What a serious policy looks like

Boards and legal teams are now asking their CISOs for notetaker policies. Having helped several organizations think through this, here is where we land.

Transparency always. If a recording tool is running, everyone present knows. The lightest version we recommend: Change your display name to “Name + AI notetaker.” And the rule must bind employees, too. An employee who records a colleague without disclosure is committing a fireable offense, full stop, before we ever discuss what the recording contains.

Classify your meetings. At one firm, we wrote a formal policy naming which meetings may never be recorded. Yours might include M&A, legal, HR, and board executive sessions. Decide deliberately, in writing, before the tools decide for you.

Govern other people’s notetakers. When an auditor walks into your building, their laptop has to meet your standards. Apply the same principle to recording. If another organization records your employees, you should know, and you should get a copy.

Choose your retention posture. A full transcript is a different corporate record than a summary. Decide whether transcripts are destroyed by default, with legal holds as the exception, or kept forever. Do not let the vendor’s default decide.

Treat notetaker vendors like what they are: startups holding your most sensitive conversations in their cloud. Vendor security review, data-reuse terms, indemnification language. Brewer v. Otter.ai, a class action alleging Otter’s notetaker recorded meetings without everyone’s consent and used the recordings to train models, and the sudden shutdown of Novacy both happened for a reason.

Assign a human. Every transcript that becomes a record needs a named owner responsible for reviewing its accuracy, no matter whose tool recorded the call.

Remember that some may train employees to steer the transcript, the way a lawyer protects the record in a deposition. We understand the instinct, and reviewing the record for accuracy is exactly right. An organization that quietly optimizes its official records has bigger problems coming.

We used to debate whether to let the notetaker into the meeting. That debate is over, because the meeting is now everywhere the recorder goes. Write your policies for the world where the microphone is already in the room, because it is.

item.title: Black October: This week’s cybersecurity crises mean infrastructure inventory just became a board-level priority
item.description:
“Are we exposed?” CIOs and CTOs heard that question all last week. On Tuesday, PHP shipped emergency fixes for two pre-authentication remote code execution flaws that date back to 2004. By Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said every supported version of PAN-OS and Panorama was vulnerable and no fix was available. Cisco was reviewing 18 products and 13 cloud services, and Fortinet was reviewing eleven. NSA, NCSC and CERT-EU told operators to take unpatched systems offline, and Cloudflare’s CEO watched exploit attempts jump from thousands to millions within hours. People are calling it Black October.

An AI model found most of these bugs. The lesson for boards, though, isn’t about AI. Patching is no longer the bottleneck. Knowing where to patch is.

“Please go to your boards and ask for help right now. Not for AI, for the basics.” (Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO, Anthropic, Oct. 22.) Marc Benioff replied: “Jason is 100% right. Code red.”

Answering “are we affected?” should take minutes. That takes one real-time, authoritative record of every device, version, site, owner and exposure, plus automation that patches from that record and confirms the fix. Organizations without that record are still searching while attackers move. With vulnerability volume climbing this fast, the gap will only grow.

The number of vulnerabilities has more than doubled in the last year – and it is just getting started

From January 1 to October 13, 79,680 CVEs were published, 2.15 times the same period in 2025. Microsoft alone published 1,408 on October 13. That’s more than it disclosed in all of 2025, and its fourth record month in a row.

AI is behind the surge. Between April and July, Anthropic’s Project Glasswing partners verified more than 129,000 vulnerabilities, over 33,000 of them critical or high, and Anthropic estimates the real total is at least five times higher. Google’s threat intelligence group says monthly disclosures doubled from January to August, and that AI-found bugs are twice as likely to be remote code execution. OpenAI, whose model found the PHP flaws, expects such findings to “increase sharply in the coming months.”

Exploitation is speeding up just as fast. Mandiant’s mean time-to-exploit for 2025 was negative seven days, and Microsoft puts median discovery-to-weaponization under 24 hours. Amazon CISO CJ Moses saw PHP2Shell probing four days before a patch existed. His warning: the disclosure date isn’t the earliest date of exploitation. Reuters reported that one operator used AI agents to breach more than 100 companies for about $5,000 in tokens. That works out to roughly $50 a breach.

Attackers can’t be allowed to have a better asset inventory than you do

Enterprises simply aren’t keeping up:

  • Verizon’s 2026 DBIR found just 26 percent of known-exploited vulnerabilities fully remediated, down from 38 percent, with a median of 43 days.
  • Moody’s puts the median at 87 days for exploited bugs.
  • Tenable found Citrix environments take a median of 461 days to patch.

The patch itself is rarely the obstacle. The obstacle is systems nobody knew about. As Armis’s threat intelligence lead put it this week, “the most common gap is not knowing an instance exists.” PHP is built into firewall consoles, NAS admin panels, printers, cameras and switches that never advertise it. Action1’s field CTO said it more bluntly: “The inventory is a guide, not a shield.” Most enterprises don’t even have the guide.

Two incidents this month show the stakes. On October 16, Palo Alto’s Unit 42 disclosed that attackers who compromised FortiManager instances got an inventory of more than 500 downstream FortiGate firewalls, including serial numbers and public IPs, and used it to gain root on those firewalls. In the Reuters case, when the target application had no flaw, the agents moved to adjacent infrastructure and found an exposed control panel nobody was watching.

AI now finds the bug, writes the exploit and maps your estate faster than your team can. The defender’s one lasting advantage is knowing the estate better than the attacker: every device, version, exposure and owner. That knowledge has to drive action in hours, not quarters.

Network and infrastructure is the front line

The hardest systems to see are the ones getting hit hardest. Google reports that edge and security appliances accounted for 14 percent of exploited vulnerabilities this year, and two-thirds of those were high or critical. Mandiant notes these devices usually lack standard EDR telemetry. In October, actively exploited flaws hit Ivanti Connect Secure, Cisco Secure Email Gateway, Palo Alto PAN-OS, Fortinet FortiMail and FortiOS, SonicWall SMA and Citrix NetScaler. Then PHP2Shell exposed the management plane of nearly every major network vendor at once.

You can’t put an agent on a router or scan what isn’t routable. That’s true across the campus, the branch and edge, the AI data center and the OT floor. The control that works there is an accurate, current record of what’s deployed, what it runs, where it sits, who owns it and whether it’s reachable from the internet, plus automation that acts on that record.

This is a board question now

Every board should ask its infrastructure leaders five questions this month:

  1. Do we have a single, continuously updated inventory of every network device, server and appliance we operate — with software version, location, owner and internet exposure?
  2. When the next PHP2Shell lands, how long does it take us to answer “which of our systems are affected”? Minutes, or weeks?
  3. Is that inventory discovered from the live network, or is it a spreadsheet someone updates when they remember?
  4. Can our automation patch directly from that inventory, or does every advisory start with a manual hunt?
  5. After we patch, do we verify the fix took and the estate hasn’t drifted?

If the answers are no, weeks, spreadsheet, manual and no, the problem isn’t patching. It’s a gap in the fundamentals, and no patch-management budget will close it.

What to do this quarter, not next year

Treat this as a loop that runs continuously, not a project with an end date:

  • Discover. Find everything on the network automatically, all the time. Unknown devices are the attacker’s favorite devices.
  • Record. Put it in one system of record: the intended state of your infrastructure, not a scan export. Version, role, site, owner, exposure.
  • Prioritize. Join that record against KEV and vendor advisories. Internet-reachable plus critical plus exploited goes first. The rest is a queue, not a panic.
  • Patch from the record. Drive automation off the inventory so a new advisory becomes a targeted job, not a scavenger hunt.
  • Verify and repeat. Confirm the live state matches the intended state, catch drift, and go again. Forever.

Automation helps teams keep pace, but without an authoritative inventory, it just misses things faster.

Attackers now discover at machine speed, while remediation still moves at the speed of someone opening a spreadsheet. Until that changes, attackers will know your infrastructure better than you do. Fix that first, and fix it this quarter.

item.title: SAP wants Joule to run business workflows, not just answer questions
item.description:
SAP says it is ushering in a new era of agentic AI, one where agents don’t just learn a business, but help run it.

This week at its TechEd conference, the company is announcing new tools in its SAP Business AI Platform that will extend AI agents’ capabilities, give them richer, more enterprise-specific data and context, and beef up governance controls so they can be rolled out safely across enterprise workflows.

“There used to be a time where AI assistants or interfaces could do a couple queries, and you had to get the query more or less right,” SAP chief AI officer Jonathan von Rüden told CIO. “And then if you asked three, four questions, eventually it would say, ‘I can’t go that far.’ Now that constraint isn’t really there anymore.”

New orchestration layer

SAP has introduced new capabilities in its AI-driven workspace Joule Work and its AI no-code/pro-code agent building environment, Joule Studio.

Joule Studio will now be natively integrated with Joule Work, giving users a single build layer. They will be able to describe their intent, and the system will orchestrate the right agents, apps, and data. Joule Work is built on the SAP Business AI Platform, which provides context, data, and governance.

“Effectively, business users get a coding agent into their hands, but they don’t know it is one, so they come up with all kinds of very, very interesting use cases,” von Rüden said.

SAP has put a good deal of R&D effort into graduating from conversations to a generative UI to “step-by-step” replace classic UIs, he noted. “You don’t need those anymore, you can have them tailor made per person.”

A new orchestration layer in Joule Work will support more complex, multi-step workflows. Beyond working across SAP environments, agents will be able to plug into external systems, data, and tools via Modern Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol.

Further, Joule Studio will be more tightly integrated with SAP Business Data Cloud so that builders can access various data products across SAP, and users across different teams will be able to collaborate on agents while customizing them to their different roles. These shared environments will have role-based access, and developers will be able to design and run n8n workflows, test pre-deployment in built-in sandboxes, and perform offline evaluations.

Governance, debugging tools

The company also announced that the SAP Knowledge Graph will now have the ability to pull data from both SAP and non-SAP sources, while interoperability tools will allow third-party agents to securely invoke Joule Agents through a governed gateway. This will enable safe collaboration between agents from different providers, SAP said.

New AI capabilities in the SAP Integration Suite will provide tools that analyze bugs, flag anomalies, simplify schema setups, manage GitHub integrations, perform core Git operations, standardize communications, and automate processes across platforms like Gmail, Microsoft Excel, and Salesforce Service Cloud.

From a governance perspective, a new SAP Enterprise AI Gateway will consolidate authentication, policy enforcement, routing, monitoring, usage tracking, and auditing, giving users the ability to view and govern all traffic and interactions. Joule Studio also has new observability and administrative controls, and a new Governance Agent will help companies comply with the EU AI Act.

The Enterprise AI Gateway will bring “enterprise-grade governance to AI interactions” in one control plane, SAP said.

SAP is rolling out Joule Work and the various new Joule Studio features in phases, and general availability for SAP Enterprise AI Gateway and the new SAP Knowledge Graph capabilities are planned for Q1 2027.

Accessing hundreds of assistants for enterprise workflows

With Joule Work and Joule Studio, users can immediately customize a skill load, von Rüden said, and can easily build a reusable dashboard. “Now they have these standard backend connections to SAP.”

For instance, he explained, say a user wants to plan deliveries for the next six weeks. They can pull in data from Jira and GitHub, but also overlay that with data from project planning. “I crunch all of this up in completely natural language, and with out of the box UIs, I can see whether I can actually deliver on what I’ve planned over the next six weeks,” he said.

If a user likes something they co-designed with AI, they can tell it to persist that workflow as a skill. “I can share it back with other colleagues, and that becomes a very powerful workflow,” von Rüden said. “I’m not queuing for eight months in the IT backlog.”

With Joule Work, users have access to 40 specific assistants that can orchestrate hundreds of agents beneath. These include, for example, billing, campaign, enterprise architecture, case management, or HR operations assistants.

“Customers can map these assistants to actual personas,” von Rüden said. Then, assistants can be connected to other relevant assistants (like accounts payable and accounts receivable). “We have one central place where they can exchange trust, and we can secure everything, do policy enforcement.”

Essentially, the right integrations can support near-infinite iteration in AI systems, von Rüden asserted.

New data tools, Tabular foundation model

Also at TechEd this week, SAP is introducing new ontology tools, lakehouse capabilities, and governance and admin controls to take AI from “intent to trusted execution.” The company is building on its recent acquisition of Dremio and an expanded partnership with Databricks to unify data, simplify its management, and support faster contextual insights.

The company is also infusing AI into RISE with SAP, its subscription-based service that helps enterprises transition from on-premises enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems to the cloud. Customers will get AI-assisted implementation guidance, best practices, roadmaps, onboarding, and assessment, alignment, and business mapping tools.

Finally, SAP has announced its latest tabular AI model, SAP-RPT-2.0, which will go beyond classification and regression to anomaly and outlier detection and AI-powered analysis. These capabilities will reduce manual engineering and help customers predict values across business metrics for forecasting purposes. Customers will be able to use SAP-RPT-2.0 through the SAP Integrated Business Planning platform.

von Rüden said that the model is being used for “so many wild use cases,” ranging from running small business loans and performing financial forecasting to the classification of astronaut health by NASA.

item.title: Developers Reporting Double-Digit Weekly Time Savings from AI Fell from 68% to 26%
item.description:
Atlassian’s State of Developer Experience 2026 finds the share of developers saving ten or more hours a week with AI dropped from 68% to 26% year over year, while only 28% report noticeably less friction than before AI. Engineering leaders report spending more time managing and correcting AI output than developers do.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
